text: Progress Iteratively With Feedback asks organizations to organize work into smaller, manageable pieces that can be completed in a timely manner, rather than attempting one sweeping initiative that tries to fix everything at once. A full platform migration, a complete process overhaul, a total rewrite of every runbook — these look efficient on a planning slide and turn genuinely risky the moment real work starts.

Big-bang initiatives compress all of their risk into one release event — if something's wrong with the plan, you don't find out until most of the investment is already spent, and by then there's little room left to course-correct cheaply. Instead, this principle pushes toward comprehending the whole but doing something smaller and well-defined, getting it done, checking the outcome, and adjusting before moving to the next piece. That checking step, the feedback, is what actually closes the loop — it isn't optional decoration.

This principle is explicitly aligned with Agile and Lean thinking — short cycles, visible progress, and a willingness to adjust direction based on what's actually learned rather than what was originally planned. ITIL 4 absorbed this logic from Agile software development, recognizing that the same reasoning that makes iterative software delivery safer also makes iterative service improvement safer, down to small details like rolling out one knowledge base section before the next.

This principle only works well in combination with the previous one. You can't define a sensible first small piece of work without first understanding the current state well enough to know what's genuinely worth tackling. The two form a sequence in practice: assess what exists, make one deliberate bounded change, measure what actually happened, and let that result inform the next bounded change.
Small pieces, real feedback, informed next steps. Next up: the fourth guiding principle, Collaborate and Promote Visibility.
